reasoning: The sink is real and unguarded. XAIWireTypes.swift:261 copies creditUsagePercent straight into UsageWindow (UsageWindow.swift:20 has no clamp). Neither UsageSnapshot.swift:70-71 (maxUtilization) nor AggregatesComputation.compute in UsageStore.swift:352 clamps it, and MenuBarLabelView.swift:41 calls Int(percent.rounded()), which traps on an out-of-range Double. That makes it a robustness bug. What fails is requirement 1, a source the attacker controls. The value comes only from the xAI billing endpoint. AppConfig.swift:715-722 (XAIConfig.validate) only accepts an https URL whose host is on allowedHosts (cli-chat-proxy.grok.com, line 661), and any rejected config value falls back to the default (lines 696-702). So the only parties who can inject 1e300 are xAI itself, with its own valid TLS certificate, or someone who can already write the user's local config and install a trusted root on the machine. Either one already has far more power than crashing a menu-bar app. The finding's own precondition is 'attacker controls the Grok CLI proxy response body', and the host allowlist plus TLS rule that out. I could not trace a third-party source to the sink, so there is no attack path. Clamping at the wire boundary is still a sensible hardening fix.
